notes.title: Steam Audio 4.1.0 Release
notes.content:
We've just released [url=https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/downloads.html]Steam Audio 4.1.0[/url]. This release includes a major update to the Steam Audio Unreal Engine plugin, bringing it up to date with the latest features of the Steam Audio SDK. This is also the first release in which the Unreal Engine plugin is released alongside the other plugins and the core SDK.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/27920370/9f293b279c8f8711bbdbe67cbce8f220b9a71d4d.png[/img]

The major new features of the Unreal Engine plugin in this release include:

[h3]FMOD Studio support[/h3]
If you are using FMOD Studio as your audio middleware in your Unreal Engine project, the Steam Audio Unreal Engine plugin now works with the Steam Audio FMOD Studio plugin. Events authored in FMOD Studio can use occlusions, reverb, etc. simulated by Steam Audio in Unreal Engine levels.

[h3]macOS and Linux support[/h3]
The Unreal Engine plugin now supports Windows (64-bit Intel), macOS (64-bit Intel), Linux (64-bit Intel), and Android (32-bit ARM, 64-bit ARM, and 32-bit Intel). Note that precompiled macOS binaries are not provided out of the box, but Unreal Engine will automatically compile the plugin for macOS when you open a project that uses the plugin. Precompiled binaries for macOS will be provided in a subsequent patch release.

[h3]Sublevel support (including streaming sublevels)[/h3]
Geometry can be tagged in any sublevel referenced by a level. Whether the sublevels are loaded automatically along with the main level, or streamed in based on a level streaming volume or any custom logic, Steam Audio will update occlusion, reflections, and reverb automatically.

[h3]Dynamic geometry in Blueprint classes[/h3]
Any Blueprint class can now be configured to be a Steam Audio dynamic object, and Steam Audio will automatically update occlusion, reflections, and reverb as instances of the Blueprint class move through your levels.

[h3]Baked data exported to .uassets[/h3]
Level geometry (both static and dynamic) as well as baked sound propagation data is now stored in .uasset files that are referenced by Steam Audio components. This simplifies the packaging workflow for your projects.

[h3]Latest Steam Audio SDK features[/h3]
In addition to the above, this release of the Steam Audio Unreal Engine plugin includes all the latest features of the core Steam Audio SDK, such as pathing, hybrid reverb, and more.

Going forward, updates to the Unreal Engine plugin will continue to be available on GitHub, including source code and pre-built binaries. The version of Steam Audio built into Unreal Engine will be periodically updated, but the latest versions will always be available on GitHub.

For the full release notes for this release, click [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio/releases/tag/v4.1.0]here[/url].

notes.title: Steam Audio 4.0.0 Release
notes.content:
We've just released [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio/releases/tag/v4.0.0]Steam Audio 4.0.0[/url], which is a major update to Steam Audio. This release includes new features and an updated API that is more flexible than previous releases. Because this is a major update, the version numbering we used so far was no longer sufficient: we have updated from 2.0-beta.20 (the previous release) to 4.0.0 (the next available integer).

This release includes features that were developed or significantly enhanced during the development of [i]Half-Life: Alyx[/i].

[url={STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/27920370/6213f1376bb7220170254ce0fcc8c81c5a1ff03b.png][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/27920370/6213f1376bb7220170254ce0fcc8c81c5a1ff03b.png[/img][/url]

The major new features in this release include:

[h3]Pathing[/h3]
Pathing is a new way of baking sound propagation from a moving source to a moving listener. This involves placing probes in the scene, and calculating shortest paths between each pair of probes. At run-time, this baked data is used to calculate how sound propagates from the moving source to the moving listener, and spatialize the sound accordingly. If a baked shortest path is occluded by dynamic geometry (like a door), Steam Audio can recalculate alternate shortest paths on the fly. Steam Audio also applies a diffraction model to paths that bend around corners or through doorways, etc. This feature is useful for modeling how sound emitted by an occluded source reaches the player through doors or windows instead of directly through walls.

[h3]Hybrid Reverb[/h3]
When rendering reflections or reverb, Steam Audio can use convolution reverb (which is defined in terms of an impulse response) or parametric reverb (which is defined in terms of a small set of parameters, like decay time). Convolution reverb results in more accurate reproduction of early reflections and directionality, but requires more CPU. Parametric reverb requires less CPU, but cannot reproduce early reflections as accurately, especially in outdoor spaces. Hybrid reverb is a hybrid of the two: the early reflections are rendered using an impulse response, and the later reverb tail is rendered using parametric reverb. The transition between the two types of reverb is smooth and controllable, as is the length of the reverb tail. This feature is useful for trading off reverb quality and performance.

[h3]Unity Plugin: Additive Scenes[/h3]
The Unity plugin now has full support for additive scenes. Multiple scenes can be opened additively in the editor, and exported separately. Scenes can be additively loaded and unloaded freely at run-time, and Steam Audio will automatically update occlusion, reflections, and pathing simulation to account for the changes.

[h3]C API Redesign[/h3]
The Steam Audio C API has been significantly redesigned, with the goal of increasing the flexibility available to developers and sound designers. Developers can control when and how often simulations are run, and can perform arbitrary post-processing before using the simulation results for rendering. For example, after simulating reverb, the length of the reverb tail can be increased or decreased based on the game state. Simulation results can also be used outside of spatial audio rendering: for example, the results of pathing simulation can be used to drive enemy AI.

Due to the major changes in the API and plugin design, this release is not backwards-compatible with previous releases. In-place upgrades are not recommended for existing projects, except those in the earliest stages of development.

This release includes updates to the Unity plugin, FMOD Studio plugin, and C API. An update to the Unreal plugin will be released separately.

For the full release notes for this release, click [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio/releases/tag/v4.0.0]here[/url].

notes.title: Beta 18: Expanded Android support, Spatial Blend
notes.content:
We've just released [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio/releases/tag/v2.0-beta.18]Steam Audio 2.0-beta.18[/url], which includes support for a wider range of CPU architectures on Android, performance and quality improvements, and several bug fixes. Below are some of the highlights.

[h1]Expanded Android Support[/h1]
Previous versions of the Steam Audio SDK have supported Android devices that can run 32-bit ARM (armv7) code only. Starting with 2.0-beta.18, the Steam Audio SDK supports a much wider range of Android devices, by providing binaries for 64-bit ARM (armv8/arm64/aarch64), 32-bit Intel (x86), and 64-bit Intel (x86_64/x64) processors as well.

The Unity plugin now supports Android builds for ARMv7, ARM64, and x86 targets. Building a Unity project for ARM64 requires the IL2CPP scripting backend.

The FMOD Studio plugin also now supports Android builds for ARMv7, ARM64, and x86 targets.

[h1]Improved Spatial Blend[/h1]
Sound designers often want to transition between using highly positional HRTF for sounds that are far enough away from the listener, and un-spatialized stereo audio clips for sounds that are very close to the listener. At Valve, we've used this approach in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, and Half-Life: Alyx. For example, the same weapon sound could be rendered with HRTF if an enemy is firing the weapon, but as a stereo clip if it's the player firing. To ensure a smooth transition between spatialized and un-spatialized audio as the listener approaches the source, we've added a new spatial blend parameter to the Steam Audio binaural effect. As the value of this parameter is ramped down from 1 to 0, the audio smoothly changes from spatialized to un-spatialized, without phasing artifacts.

This functionality is also available in the Unity plugin. To use it, just adjust the Spatial Blend slider on Unity's built-in Audio Source component. Refer to the documentation for more details.

[h1]Release Notes[/h1]
The full release notes for this release are [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio/releases]here.[/url]

notes.title: Beta 17: Unreal Engine 4.24 Update
notes.content:
We've recently updated the Steam® Audio Unreal Engine integration with the latest Beta 17 API. This version will be part-and-parcel of UE 4.24 and bolsters Steam® Audio performance with support for [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/596420/announcements/detail/1681419156989838545]multi-threaded environmental effect simulation[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/596420/announcements/detail/1674659226616741624]Intel® Embree[/url], and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/596420/announcements/detail/1681419156989664451]AMD Radeon Rays[/url].

Each of these features provide developers with significant performance boosts compared to simulating environmental effects with the built-in Steam® Audio raytracer on a single thread. Radeon Rays, which runs on any OpenCL 1.2 compatible GPU, can provide 50-150X speed-ups. Intel® Embree, which runs on the CPU, can provide speed-ups of around 20X when using recent 4-core CPUs. The built-in raytracer also benefits significantly from the new multi-threading support and its performance scales linearly with the number of threads.

notes.title: Beta 17: Dual Reserved Queue Support with Radeon Rays
notes.content:
We've just released [url=https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/downloads.html]Steam® Audio 2.0-beta.17[/url], which includes several new features, including support for real-time indirect sound simulation using AMD Radeon™ Rays. Previously, Radeon™ Rays was supported only for baking. With this release, Radeon™ Rays and AMD TrueAudio Next can be combined to perform indirect sound simulation and rendering on the GPU without interfering with graphics or general GPU compute. This blog post discusses how this works.

[h1]Previously, on Steam® Audio...[/h1]
Over the last few releases, we have added features to the Steam® Audio that enable the GPU to be used in different ways for accelerating spatial audio computations.

In 2.0-beta.13, [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/596420/announcements/detail/1647624403070736393]we added support for TrueAudio Next[/url]. This feature uses the Resource Reservation capability of supported AMD GPUs to carve out a portion of the GPU (called a "reserved queue") dedicated to audio convolution processing. This allows the GPU to be used for significantly speeding up spatial audio rendering, while ensuring that audio and graphics do not interfere with each other. The result is stable graphics frame rates, and fast, glitch-free audio processing.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2561bbd971cf7f25e9d4d9395614ef6a9e53da45.png[/img]
[i][b]Figure:[/b] Impact on GPU rendering performance when reserving 4 CUs for TrueAudio Next processing. The plots show the average FPS observed on various GPU benchmarks when run at the same time as a TAN benchmark using Steam®® Audio. Measurements obtained using a Radeon™ RX 480 GPU with 4 reserved CUs, 256 total convolution channels and 1.3s IRs. All values are shown as a percentage of a baseline that is obtained when the TAN benchmark is not running. For example, reserving 10% of the available CUs reduces the average FPS in the Timespy benchmark by about 10%.[/i]

In 2.0-beta.15, [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/596420/announcements/detail/1681419156989664451]we added support for Radeon™ Rays[/url]. This feature runs on any GPU supporting OpenCL 1.2 or later, and uses the GPU to accelerate indirect sound simulation (ray tracing and related processing). Since the reserved queue was used by TrueAudio Next, Radeon™ Rays would run on the remainder of the GPU, along with graphics and general compute. If used for real-time simulation, it would therefore interfere with graphics frame rates, which is why this feature was restricted to baking only.

[h1]What's new?[/h1]
Starting with AMD Radeon™ Software Adrenalin 2019 Edition v19.2.1, AMD GPUs support up to two reserved queues. In other words, the GPU compute units can be divided into three sets: 2 reserved queues, and 1 general queue. This feature (called "Dual RTQ") only requires a driver update.

In 2.0-beta.17, Steam® Audio runs Radeon™ Rays on the second reserved queue, thereby isolating indirect sound simulation from graphics as well. This way simulation (using Radeon™ Rays), convolution (using TrueAudio Next), and graphics can all be run on the same GPU without interfering with each other. This results in stable frame rates, glitch-free audio processing, and low-latency indirect sound simulation.

[h1]How Dual RTQ works[/h1]
As an example, consider a Radeon™ RX Vega 64, which contains 64 Compute Units (CUs). A maximum of 16 CUs (25% of the GPU) can be used in all reserved queues combined. One way to partition this would be:
[list]
[*]First reserved queue, 4 CUs. Used by TrueAudio Next.
[*]Second reserved queue, 8 CUs. Used by Radeon™ Rays.
[*]Remainder of the GPU, 52 CUs. Used for graphics and general compute.
[/list]
This can be set up using the Steam® Audio Unity Plugin as follows. Begin by attaching a Steam® Audio Custom Settings component to the Steam® Audio Manager Settings GameObject. Then in the Inspector tab, configure it as follows:

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/947976eef6027bf963b5951781c9d0fe6e333474.png[/img]
[list]
[*]Set [b]Max Compute Units To Reserve[/b] to 12. This is the total number of CUs used in both reserved queues combined (4 for TrueAudio Next + 8 for Radeon™ Rays).
[*]Set [b]Fraction Compute Units for IR Update[/b] to 0.67 (approximately 2/3). This is the fraction of reserved CUs to be used for Radeon™ Rays. (0.67 * 12 total reserved CUs = 8 CUs for Radeon™ Rays).
[/list]
The remaining 52 CUs will be used for graphics and general compute.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Below are representative speedup numbers for various simulation scenarios with varying numbers of CUs reserved for Radeon™ Rays. All measurements were obtained on an Intel® Core i7 5930K (Haswell E) CPU, along with an AMD Radeon™ RX Vega 64 GPU, running Windows 10 64-bit and AMD Radeon™ Software Adrenalin 2019 Edition v19.2.1.

notes.title: Beta 16: Custom HRTF Support
notes.content:
In the spatial audio community, there is a lot of interesting, ongoing research and experimentation that aims to understand the trade-offs involved in using customized (or personalized) HRTFs. With the latest release of [url=https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/downloads.html]Steam Audio 2.0-beta.16[/url], we want to provide developers with an efficient tool that enables them to conduct experiments and research studies. Our hope is that new knowledge in this domain can be created faster, and can be shared with the VR and gaming communities more easily.

Custom HRTFs can be specified to Steam Audio using the SOFA file format. SOFA stands for Spatially-Oriented Format for Acoustics, and is a standard developed by the Audio Engineering Society (AES) and published in 2015. For more information on the SOFA format, see [url=https://www.sofaconventions.org/]https://www.sofaconventions.org/[/url].

How to obtain a SOFA file, whether by measurement, calibration, or any other process, is beyond the scope of Steam Audio. We just provide an efficient tool for using SOFA files for research and experimentation.

Steam Audio makes a few assumptions about the data provided using SOFA files; for more information refer to the documentation.

To provide a SOFA file to Steam Audio, follow the instructions below.

[h1]Unity plugin[/h1]
Copy SOFA files to the StreamingAssets directory in your Unity project. Then open the Steam Audio tab (Window > Steam Audio) and specify the SOFA files to load under HRTF Settings.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/25d3bfe08e59f32678dcd5036f2c4473d7bacb9b.png[/img]

[h1]FMOD Studio plugin[/h1]
SOFA files are specified using your game engine. If using Unity, follow the instructions for the Unity plugin; the FMOD Studio plugin will automatically load and use your SOFA files.

[h1]Unreal plugin[/h1]
SOFA file support will be added to the Unreal plugin in an upcoming update.

[h1]C API[/h1]
SOFA files are loaded when creating a Binaural Renderer using iplCreateBinauralRenderer. The relevant information is passed using the params parameter to this function: set the type member to IPL_HRTFDATABASETYPE_SOFA and the sofaFileName member to the absolute path to the SOFA file you wish to load.

For more information on using any of the above plugins to load SOFA files, refer to the relevant documentation. Note that SOFA files are not necessary to use Steam Audio; you can continue to use Steam Audio for HRTF-based 3D audio and all of its other features without specifying any SOFA files, just as before.

notes.title: Beta 15: Radeon Rays support
notes.content:
We have just released Steam Audio 2.0 beta 15, which brings support for AMD Radeon Rays technology. Radeon Rays is a high-performance, GPU-accelerated software library for ray tracing, and works on any modern AMD, NVIDIA, or other GPU. Steam Audio uses ray tracing when baking indirect sound propagation and reverberation; using Radeon Rays lets Steam Audio achieve performance gains of 50x-150x over the built-in ray tracer running with a single thread during baking. For example, reverb bakes that required an hour using the built-in ray tracer with a single thread should now take less than a minute using Radeon Rays on a Radeon RX Vega 64 GPU.

Radeon Rays support is optional in Steam Audio; Steam Audio continues to work on any PC with any CPU or GPU, as well as on ARM-based Android devices.

[h1]How is Radeon Rays useful to Steam Audio?[/h1]
Steam Audio uses ray tracing for baking indirect sound propagation. Rays are traced from a probe position and bounced around the scene until they hit a source. The surfaces hit by the rays determine how much energy is absorbed, and how much reaches the probe from the source. These energies, along with the arrival times of each ray, are used to construct the impulse response from the source to the probe. An impulse response (IR) is an audio filter that represents the acoustics of the scene; rendering a sound with the IR creates the impression that the sound was emitted from within the scene.

The above approach is also used when baking reverb; in this case rays are traced from a probe position and bounced around the scene until they hit the probe again. The IR constructed this way models the listener-centric reverb at the probe position.

When baking, ray tracing is used to simulate indirect sound propagation for hundreds, or even thousands of probes for a typical scene. Radeon Rays lets developers use the compute capabilities of their GPU to significantly accelerate baking, resulting in measurable time savings during the design process.

The current release of Steam Audio does not support real-time simulation with Radeon Rays.

[h1]What is Radeon Rays?[/h1]
Radeon Rays is a software library that provides GPU-accelerated algorithms for tracing coherent rays (direct light) and incoherent rays (global illumination, sound propagation). Radeon Rays is highly optimized for modern GPUs, and provides OpenCL and Vulkan backends. Steam Audio uses the OpenCL backend, which requires a GPU that supports OpenCL 1.2 or higher.

Radeon Rays is not restricted to AMD hardware; it works with any device that supports OpenCL 1.2 or higher, including NVIDIA and Intel GPUs.

[h1]What are the benefits of Radeon Rays?[/h1]
When using Steam Audio to bake indirect sound propagation or reverb, Radeon Rays provides significant speedups and time savings for designers:

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/30b33a9ee35eedc3773ded1de7dc10ded49f0093.png[/img]
[i][b]Figure:[/b] Speedup when baking reverb using Radeon Rays vs. Embree (single-threaded) vs. Steam Audio's built-in ray tracer (single-threaded), for two scenes: Sibenik cathedral (80k triangles) and a Hangar scene from the Unity Asset Store (140k triangles). Speedups are averaged over a range of simulation settings and probe grid densities, and plotted using a logarithmic scale. Speedups shown in the graph are relative to Steam Audio's built-in ray tracer. For example, on the Sibenik cathedral, Embree on a single core is 5.2x faster than the built-in ray tracer on a single core; Radeon Rays on an RX Vega 64 is 153.9x faster than the built-in ray tracer on a single core.[/i]

The above performance measurements were obtained on an Intel Core i7 5930K (Haswell E) CPU, along with an AMD Radeon RX Vega 64 GPU, running Windows 10 64-bit.

[h1]How do I enable Radeon Rays in Steam Audio?[/h1]

[b]System Requirements[/b]
Radeon Rays support in Steam Audio is requires a GPU that OpenCL 1.2 or higher. Tested GPUs include: AMD Radeon RX Vega 64, AMD Radeon R9 Nano, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti.

Radeon Rays support in Steam Audio is available on Windows (64-bit).

[b]Using the Unity plugin[/b]
To use Radeon Rays in a Unity project that uses the Steam Audio Unity plugin, you must add a [b]Steam Audio Custom Settings[/b] component to the [b]Steam Audio Manager Settings[/b] object in every scene that you wish to use Radeon Rays in, and then set [b]Ray Tracer Option[/b] to [b]Radeon Rays[/b]. Refer to the documentation for more details.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/b6c50364a767c36fa2cc9d3a65ab00c5233df2c7.png[/img]

[b]Using the C API[/b]
To use Radeon Rays in an application that directly uses the Steam Audio C API, you will need to perform the following main steps:
[olist]
[*] [b]Initialize an OpenCL compute device.[/b] To do this, call iplCreateComputeDevice, typically at application startup. This will cause Steam Audio to try initializing OpenCL. If no supported device is found on the user's PC, an error code is returned. The application should test this error code and take appropriate action in case of failure, such as falling back to Steam Audio's built-in CPU-based ray tracer. This compute device should be passed to all Steam Audio API functions that take a computeDevice parameter.
[*] [b]Create a Scene that uses Radeon Rays for ray tracing.[/b] When calling iplCreateScene or iplLoadFinalizedScene to create a Scene, in the simulationSettings parameter, set sceneType to IPL_SCENETYPE_RADEONRAYS.
[*] [b]Configure how probes are baked.[/b] In the simulationSettings parameter, set bakingBatchSize to the number of probes that should be simultaneously baked on the GPU. Typical values are in the range of 2-4, but higher values may yield better performance on more powerful GPUs.
[/olist]

[b]Other Integrations[/b]
Radeon Rays support will be enabled in the Steam Audio plugins for FMOD Studio and Unreal Engine 4 in an upcoming release.

notes.title: Source Directivity in Steam Audio
notes.content:
One of the new features introduced in Steam Audio 2.0-beta.14 is [i]source directivity[/i]. In the real world, sources emit sounds with different intensities in different directions. For example, when a person is speaking, their speech is louder in front of them than behind them. Source directivity is a way of modeling this phenomenon in virtual worlds.

[h1]Directivity affects reflections[/h1]
Usually, source directivity only affects sound traveling in a straight line from the source to the listener. In Steam Audio, every individual reflection of sound is affected by source directivity, opening up new opportunities for designers. For example, the below video shows a rotating source with a cardioid directivity. When the source emits sound into the reverberant room, reverb can be heard at the listener position; when the source emits sound away from the reverberant room, almost no reverb is heard.

https://youtu.be/VRS2rpC3LKg

[h1]How does directivity work?[/h1]
A source directivity pattern specifies a scaling factor to be applied to sound as a function of direction relative to the source's coordinate system. The default directivity pattern in Steam Audio is a weighted sum of an omnidirectional (monopole) pattern and a dipole pattern oriented along the source's z-axis (front/back axis). This directivity pattern is controlled by two numbers: the [i]dipole weight[/i], and the [i]dipole power[/i]. The dipole weight determines how "dipole-like" the final directivity pattern is: setting this to 0 gives an omnidirectional pattern, setting this to 1 gives a pure dipole pattern, and setting this to 0.5 gives a front-facing cardioid pattern. The dipole power determines how "sharp" or "focused" the dipole is.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/7872fb391b4c660bf086e94ae6e94efcadb62e68.png[/img]

[h1]Using directivity in Steam Audio[/h1]

[b]Unity Plugin[/b]
To use source directivity in the Unity plugin, first attach a Steam Audio Source component to the Audio Source you want to specify a directivity pattern for. Next, use the Dipole Weight and Dipole Power sliders to specify the directivity pattern; the visualization will update in the Inspector tab and in the Scene tab as you adjust the sliders.

[b]C API[/b]
In the C API, directivity patterns are specified using the IPLDirectivity struct, an instance of which is contained in the IPLSource struct. The IPLSource struct, in turn, is passed to the iplGetDirectSoundPath function (when simulating direct sound), and the iplSetDryAudioForConvolutionEffect function (when simulating indirect sound). Use the dipoleWeight and dipolePower member variables of the IPLDirectivity struct to specify a directivity pattern.

[h1]Arbitrary Directivity Patterns[/h1]
When using the C API, you can specify any arbitrary directivity pattern using a callback function: set the callback and userData member variables of the IPLDirectivity struct to use this functionality. The specified callback will be called by Steam Audio whenever it needs to evaluate a directivity pattern. Refer to the C API documentation for more details.

notes.title: Beta 14: Embree Support
notes.content:
[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/c9229b03b5ad7a00b99c712b533d4862344fb796.jpg[/img]

We have just released Steam® Audio 2.0 beta 14, which brings support for [url=http://embree.github.io/]Intel® Embree[/url] technology. Embree is a high-performance software library for ray tracing. Steam® Audio uses ray tracing to simulate sound propagation, occlusion, transmission, and reverberation; using Embree lets Steam® Audio achieve performance gains of 4-6x during real-time simulation and baking. For example, reverb bakes that required half an hour using the built-in ray tracer should now take just about 5 minutes with Embree. Real-time simulation that updated 2 times per second with the built-in ray tracer should now update about 8-10 times per second with Embree.

Click [url=https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/downloads.html]here[/url] to download the latest version of Steam® Audio, or click [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio]here[/url] to grab the source code for the plugins.

Embree support is optional in Steam® Audio; Steam® Audio continues to work on any PC with any CPU (with or without Embree), as well as on ARM-based Android devices (without Embree).

[h1]How is Embree useful to Steam® Audio?[/h1]
Steam® Audio uses ray tracing for simulating occlusion, transmission, and reflection of sound. Rays are traced from the listener (typically the player) to a sound source to find out if it is occluded by a solid object. The material properties of these occluding surfaces are also used to figure out how much sound, if any, is transmitted through the surfaces.

To simulate reflections, rays are traced from the listener and bounced around the scene until they hit one or more sources. The surfaces hit by the rays determine how much energy is absorbed, and how much reaches the listener from the source. These energies, along with the arrival times of each ray, are used to construct the [i]impulse response[/i] from the source to the listener. An impulse response (IR) is an audio filter that represents the acoustics of the scene; rendering a sound with the IR creates the impression that the sound was emitted from within the scene.

The above approach is also used when simulating reverb from the player's position. Baking indirect sound or reverb involves calculating IRs for many positions when designing the scene rather than when playing the game.

The performance impact of ray tracing is felt as [i]latency[/i] in Steam® Audio. If ray tracing takes too long, then there may be an observable delay between something changing on-screen, and the corresponding IR updating. For example, if a source moves from a small room to a large room, and ray tracing takes too long, the audio may not update to sound like it's coming from a large room until a few frames after the source enters the large room. The high performance ray tracing enabled by Embree allows Steam® Audio to simulate more sources in greater detail without introducing noticeable latency in IR updates.

[h1]What is Embree?[/h1]
Embree contains efficient data structures and algorithms for tracing coherent rays (direct light) and incoherent rays (global illumination, sound propagation). Embree is highly optimized for SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) instructions present in modern CPUs based on the x86 (32-bit) and x86_64 (64-bit) architectures. In particular, Embree can use SSE2, SSE4, AVX, or AVX2 instructions, depending on the capabilities of the user's CPU. Embree delivers a greater performance boost on AVX- and AVX2-capable CPUs, as compared to SSE2- or SSE4-capable CPUs.

For additional performance gains, we also rewrote portions of our reflection simulation algorithm using the [url=https://ispc.github.io/]Intel® SPMD Program Compiler (ISPC)[/url]. SPMD here refers to Single Program, Multiple Data, i.e., an abstraction where code is written as if it were designed for serial, non-SIMD execution, but the compiler transforms the code to use SIMD instructions automatically. ISPC is built as a set of extensions to C, and it was relatively straightforward to convert selected portions of Steam® Audio code to ISPC. For maximum compatibility, our ISPC code is designed to run on CPUs supporting SSE2, SSE4, AVX, or AVX2 instructions.

[h1]What are the benefits of Embree?[/h1]
When using Steam® Audio for real-time simulation of reverb or sound propagation, Embree results in significant speedups over Steam® Audio's built-in ray tracer. This lets games simulate sound propagation for more sources, in greater detail, and with lower latency, resulting in increased immersion.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/d8b9a9386b7f1cb10f259f842122d3cf7cd75475.png[/img]
[b]Figure[/b]: [i]Performance of real-time indirect sound simulation when using Embree vs. when using Steam® Audio's built-in ray tracer (Phonon), in the Sibenik cathedral scene. Simulation settings, i.e., number of rays, number of bounces, and number of sources, are varied; IR duration and Ambisonics order are kept constant at 2 seconds and 1st order, respectively. Numbers above the bars indicate speedup of Embree over Phonon.[/i]

Similarly, when using Steam® Audio for baking reverb or sound propagation, Embree results in a significant time savings for designers.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/91dea72a796a4549e79e277770f1f4803d30c98f.png[/img]
[b]Figure[/b]: [i]Time taken for baking reverb when using Embree vs. when using Steam® Audio's built-in ray tracer (Phonon), for different scenes: a simple Box, the Sibenik cathedral (80k triangles), and a Hangar scene from the Unity Asset Store (140k triangles). Simulation settings are 32768 rays, 64 bounces, 2 second IR duration, 1st order Ambisonics, and a grid spacing of about 3.7 meters. Numbers inside the orange bars indicate speedup of Embree over Phonon.[/i]

[b]All of the above performance numbers were obtained on an Intel Core i7 5930K (Haswell E) CPU, using a single thread, running Windows 10 64-bit.[/b]

[h1]How do I enable Embree in Steam® Audio?[/h1]

[b]System Requirements[/b]
Embree support in Steam Audio® is available on Windows (64-bit), Linux (64-bit), and macOS (64-bit). Embree support on macOS is available only on Macs released in 2011 or later. Note that even though the Steam® Audio binaries are universal binaries on macOS, Embree support will only work when your application is run in 64-bit mode.

[b]Using the Unity Plugin[/b]
To use Embree in a Unity project that uses the Steam® Audio Unity plugin, you must add a [b]Steam® Audio Custom Settings[/b] component to the [b]Steam® Audio Manager Settings[/b] object in every scene that you wish to use Embree in, and then set [b]Ray Tracer Option[/b] to [b]Embree[/b]. Refer to the documentation for more details.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/4d068681e25ffd280c1124f575b6d1f30d0829e2.png[/img]

[b]Using the FMOD Studio Plugin[/b]
Embree support will enabled in the Steam® Audio FMOD Studio plugin in an upcoming release.

[b]Using the Unreal Engine 4 Plugin[/b]
Embree support will be enabled in the Steam® Audio Unreal Engine 4 plugin in an upcoming release.

[b]Using the C API[/b]
To use Embree in an application that directly uses the Steam® Audio C API, you will need to create a Scene that uses Embree for ray tracing. When calling iplCreateScene or iplLoadFinalizedScene to create a Scene, in the simulationSettings parameter, set sceneType to IPL_SCENETYPE_EMBREE. If the function returns a status code indicating success, then all simulation carried out using the Scene object will use Embree. For more details, refer to the Steam® Audio SDK documentation.

notes.title: Beta 13: AMD TrueAudio Next Support
notes.content:
[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/75a499beb1d37b917faf369cd69342d895927968.jpg[/img]

We have just released Steam Audio 2.0 beta 13, which brings support for AMD TrueAudio Next technology. TrueAudio Next lets developers accelerate certain spatial audio processing tasks by reserving a portion of the GPU. Combined with Steam Audio's ability to model a wide range of acoustic phenomena, this enables increased acoustic complexity and an increased sense of presence in games and VR applications. Click [url=https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/downloads.html]here[/url] to download the latest version of Steam Audio, or click [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio]here[/url] to grab the source code for the Unity and FMOD Studio plugins.

[h1]What is TrueAudio Next?[/h1]
AMD TrueAudio Next (TAN) is a software library that implements high-performance convolution – a filtering technique – for audio data on supported GPUs. TrueAudio Next also provides a feature called Resource Reservation, which allows developers to dedicate a portion of the GPU's computational resources to be spent on time-sensitive tasks such as audio processing. Here is a brief explanation of both of these high-level features of TAN.

[b]Convolution[/b]
In the context of audio, convolution is a mathematical operation that transforms one audio signal into another. It is essentially a specific kind of filtering. A very wide range of audio filters can be implemented using convolution, including echoes, frequency equalization, HRTF-based 3D audio, reverb, and more. When using convolution, an audio filter is expressed in terms of its impulse response (IR), which can be manually specified, recorded (as is often the case when using convolution for reverb), or calculated by a simulation algorithm (as is the case with Steam® Audio).

Audio engines used for games and VR usually support convolution reverb: various combinations of audio data can be filtered using convolution, to add reverb, after the user has specified an IR in some way. This is usually real-time convolution, which means that audio is filtered as it is being played. IRs used for reverb are often quite long: representing the IR for an airplane hangar with a 5-second reverb at a 48 kHz sampling rate requires (5 * 48000) = 240,000 audio samples = around 935 KB. Real-time convolution is a very compute-intensive operation, and audio engines usually allow only 2-4 convolution reverb filters running simultaneously, to keep CPU usage within acceptable limits. Convolution reverb can model a wide range of acoustic phenomena, and leads to an increased sense of presence, which is especially important in VR. However, because it is a compute-intensive algorithm, it is often avoided in favor of less compute-intensive, less detailed reverb algorithms.

TAN uses the GPU compute capabilities of supported AMD GPUs to accelerate convolution, allowing developers to increase the acoustic complexity and detail in their games and VR applications using convolution reverb.

[b]Resource Reservation[/b]
TAN also provides a feature called resource reservation, which allows developers to reserve a portion of the GPU exclusively for audio processing. GPUs are made up of several CUs; these are roughly the GPU equivalent of the multiple cores in a CPU. It is not possible to reserve groups of cores on a CPU for one process, but with AMD resource reservation, this becomes possible for the GPU's cores. A typical high-end GPU might have 36 CUs, for example. Usually, a game's renderer uses all available CUs.

With Resource Reservation, developers can reserve some small number, say 4, of the CUs for audio processing only. This dedicates 4 CUs for audio processing, while reducing the number of CUs available to the renderer by 4. Resource reservation does not allow more than 20 to 25% of the GPU CUs to be reserved.

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/a3c651be6b4d9e962ba9dbff7ce7ea7c75557d7f.jpg[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Reserving Compute Units (CUs) with TrueAudio Next.[/i]

[b]What TrueAudio Next Is NOT[/b]
TrueAudio Next currently does not perform ray tracing for sound. Ray tracing is one way of simulating acoustic phenomena and calculating an IR; TAN focuses on accelerating the task of filtering audio data using IR after the IR has been calculated (or manually specified).

In 2013, AMD introduced TrueAudio technology, which used dedicated DSP hardware available on certain AMD GPUs to accelerate some audio functions such as rendering 3D audio using Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTFs), and convolution with static IRs. In contrast, TrueAudio Next uses standard, existing Radeon™ GPU resources to implement more general and highly scalable convolution algorithms, which can be used for a wider range of filters, including convolution reverb with time-varying IRs. As a software library built using OpenCL, TrueAudio Next can also be targeted to CPUs, but it is especially beneficial when it is used with GPU Resource Reservation.

[h1]How is TrueAudio Next useful to Steam® Audio?[/h1]

[b]Indirect Sound[/b]
Steam® Audio uses physics-based simulation to model two ways in which sound travels from a source to a listener. Direct sound is sound that travels in a straight line from the source to the listener, possibly passing through solid objects. Indirect sound is sound that is emitted from the source, bounces off solid objects repeatedly, and then reaches the listener.

Steam® Audio models indirect sound by calculating an IR using ray tracing. This IR is then used in a convolution reverb effect to add indirect sound effects to either individual sound sources (in the case of source-centric convolution reverb) or a submix of sound reaching the listener (in the case of listener-centric convolution reverb).

Simulating and rendering indirect sound is the most computationally intensive part of what Steam® Audio does, and TrueAudio Next helps manage this workload.

[b]Ambisonics[/b]
Source-centric convolution reverb can be directional in nature: somebody else's distant footsteps heard through an open doorway sound more directional than one's own footsteps in a large room, for example. Steam® Audio uses Ambisonics to represent the directional variation of indirect sound. The higher the Ambisonics order, the more spatial detail that can be rendered in the indirect sound. On the other hand, the higher the Ambisonics order, the more IRs that are needed in the convolution reverb effect. For example, 2nd order Ambisonics requires 9 convolutions per source. This too, increases the computational cost of indirect sound.

Note that Steam® Audio does not use TrueAudio Next for applying HRTF-based 3D audio rendering. The computational cost of HRTF processing is significantly lower than that of convolution reverb: thousands of sources can be rendered with HRTF-based 3D audio using a single CPU core.

[h1]Why does Steam® Audio support TrueAudio Next?[/h1]
Steam® Audio's existing CPU-based convolution has sufficient performance for many applications, particularly those that rely heavily on listener-centric reverb. However, with TrueAudio Next, Steam® Audio can offer more flexibility to developers.

There are two main reasons why we chose to support TrueAudio Next in Steam® Audio:
[list]
[*]If we can provide developers with more flexibility in choosing how their audio processing workloads are balanced on a user's PC, we want to do that. TrueAudio Next allows developers to choose how CPU and GPU resources work together to provide a compelling audio experience on the user's PC.
[*]If we can allow developers to offer an optional higher level of audio detail with their existing content on PCs that are powerful enough, we want to do that. With Steam® Audio, developers just specify higher settings to be used if a TAN-capable GPU is installed on the user's PC. Developers do not have to re-author any content to work with TAN. Steam® Audio can be used to seamlessly select either CPU- or GPU-based convolution, depending on the user's hardware configuration.
[/list]
Steam® Audio's support for TrueAudio Next does not in any way restrict Steam® Audio to specific hardware or platforms. We hope that our support for TrueAudio Next encourages hardware and platform vendors to provide more options for developers to balance their audio workloads against graphics, physics, and other workloads, which in turn will help them create better audio experiences for their users.

[h1]What are the benefits of TrueAudio Next?[/h1]

[b]Benefits of GPU convolution[/b]
TAN's OpenCL convolution algorithms move convolution from the CPU to the GPU, and help achieve significant audio processing speedups. This has the following advantages:
[list]
[*]Steam® Audio's CPU-based convolution is highly efficient, and is sufficient for a wide variety of games and VR applications, especially if only using listener-centric reverb. However, TAN allows us to give developers the option of reaching an even higher level of auditory complexity: increasing the number of sources, or the Ambisonics order for indirect sound, or the IR length, etc.
[*]By moving convolution from the CPU to the GPU, the fraction of time spent by the CPU on audio processing can be kept within the CPU budget chosen by the developer. This also frees up more CPU resources for use by other tasks such as physics simulation or AI.
[/list]
[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/52ec0cfcccdbec88f80b1c0ca8e5cb237abc56fb.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]GPU convolution performance vs CPU convolution performance, for 1s IRs, 1st order Ambisonics, 1024-sample frames, and a 48 kHz sampling rate. The performance advantage of GPU convolution increases with number of sources. CPU convolution is usable up to a moderate number of sources; GPU convolution is necessary for large numbers of sources.[/i]

[b]Benefits of resource reservation[/b]
Resource reservation causes TAN's convolution algorithms to run in isolation from any rendering, physics, or other tasks that the GPU is being used for. This has two broad advantages:
[list]
[*]Increasing the number of reserved CUs predictably results in improved performance, even under the heaviest workloads.
[*]Because audio processing does not interfere with graphics, the audio processing does not result in sudden frame rate drops and stuttering.
[*]Because graphics does not interfere with audio processing, rendering a complex scene cannot cause audio processing to slow down, which in turn helps avoid unacceptable clicks, pops, or other audio glitches.
[/list]

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2a62f348cc3fd0ef418e1c072bfd4c09f4626127.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Performance improvements with increasing numbers of reserved CUs, for 1s IRs, 1st order Ambisonics, 1024-sample frames, and a 48 kHz sampling rate. The plot shows the maximum number of sources that can be processed within a 6ms budget. Increasing the number of reserved CUs allows more sources to be processed within the same amount of time.[/i]

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2561bbd971cf7f25e9d4d9395614ef6a9e53da45.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Impact on GPU rendering performance when reserving 4 CUs for TrueAudio Next processing. The plots show the average FPS observed on various GPU benchmarks when run at the same time as a TAN benchmark using Steam® Audio. Measurements obtained using a Radeon™ RX 480 GPU with 4 reserved CUs, 256 total convolution channels and 1.3s IRs. All values are shown as a percentage of a baseline that is obtained when the TAN benchmark is not running. For example, reserving 10% of the available CUs reduces the average FPS in the Timespy benchmark by about 10%.[/i]

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/6a8f38ac7fe4a422ded8afa46b1b99851207206c.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Impact on TAN processing time when heavy graphics workloads are running concurrently. CU reservation limits the impact of heavy graphics workloads on time-sensitive audio processing tasks on the GPU. Measurements obtained using a Radeon™ RX 480 GPU with 4 reserved CUs, 256 total convolution channels, 1.3s IRs, 1024-sample audio frames, and a sampling rate of 48 kHz.[/i]

[h1]How do I enable TrueAudio Next in Steam® Audio?[/h1]

[b]System Requirements[/b]

[table]
[tr]
[th]Supported GPUs[/th]
[th]Operating System[/th]
[th]GPU Drivers[/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]Radeon™ RX 470 Series
Radeon™ RX 480 Series
Radeon™ RX 570 Series
Radeon™ RX 580 Series
Radeon™ R9 Fury
Radeon™ R9 Fury X
Radeon™ Pro Duo
Radeon™ RX Vega 56
Radeon™ RX Vega 64[/td]
[td]Windows 10, 64-bit[/td]
[td]Current Radeon™ Adrenalin Edition drivers

Download location:
[url=http://support.amd.com/en-us/download]http://support.amd.com/en-us/download[/url]
[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[b]Using the Unity Plugin[/b]
To use TAN in a Unity project that uses the Steam® Audio Unity plugin, you must add a Steam® Audio Custom Settings component to the Steam® Audio Manager Settings object in every scene that you wish to use TAN in, and then set Convolution Option to TrueAudio Next. Refer to the documentation for more details on the other settings that are displayed when Convolution Option is set to TrueAudio Next.

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2e44bdcfadb466b163d04099ac5bc15d0bc0fce1.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Enabling TrueAudio Next in the Steam® Audio Unity plugin.[/i]

Steam® Audio allows the developer to select the number of CUs to be reserved and to independently configure the higher-detail settings to be used when TrueAudio Next is available. When TrueAudio Next is not available, CPU convolution with a default configuration can be used seamlessly. TrueAudio Next, along with resource reservation, can also be enabled or disabled on a scene-by-scene basis.

[b]Using the FMOD Studio Plugin[/b]
To use TAN in an FMOD Studio project that is part of a Unity project that uses Steam® Audio FMOD Studio plugin, follow the instructions for enabling TAN in the Steam® Audio Unity plugin. No further action is required.

[b]Using the Unreal Engine 4 Plugin[/b]
To use TAN in an Unreal Engine 4 project, you can simply configure the Steam® Audio plugin settings to use convolution type "AMD TrueAudio Next". This will allow you to configure the number of compute units available for audio processing. No further action is required. 

TAN for Steam® Audio is currently available to users who build from source via [url=https://github.com/EpicGames/UnrealEngine/pull/4478]this pull request on GitHub[/url] (requires membership in the EpicGames organization).

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/6f02467ae0fac0518188c272ff02ad3c6bc5cb25.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Enabling TrueAudio Next in the Steam® Audio Unreal Engine plugin.[/i]

[b]Using the C API[/b]
To use TAN in an application that directly uses the Steam® Audio C API, you will need to perform two main steps:
[list]
[*][b]Initialize an OpenCL compute device that supports TAN.[/b] To do this, call iplCreateComputeDevice, typically at application startup. In the deviceFilter parameter, set type to IPL_COMPUTEDEVICE_GPU, and requiresTrueAudioNext to IPL_TRUE. This will cause Steam® Audio to try initializing OpenCL to use a GPU that supports TAN. If no such device is found on the user's PC, an error code is returned. The application should test this error code and take appropriate action in case of failure, such as falling back to Steam® Audio's built-in CPU-based convolution. This compute device should be passed to all Steam® Audio API functions that take a computeDevice parameter.

[*][b]Create an Environmental Renderer that uses TAN for convolution.[/b] When calling iplCreateEnvironmentalRenderer to create an environmental renderer, in the renderingSettings parameter, set convolutionType to IPL_CONVOLUTIONTYPE_TRUEAUDIONEXT. If the function returns a status code indicating success, then all subsequently created Convolution Effect objects will use TAN.
[/list]
Note that when using TAN for convolution, iplGetMixedEnvironmentalAudio is much more efficient than calling iplGetWetAudioForConvolutionEffect for each Convolution Effect object separately.

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/a3c651be6b4d9e962ba9dbff7ce7ea7c75557d7f.jpg[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Reserving Compute Units (CUs) with TrueAudio Next.[/i]

[b]What TrueAudio Next Is NOT[/b]
TrueAudio Next currently does not perform ray tracing for sound. Ray tracing is one way of simulating acoustic phenomena and calculating an IR; TAN focuses on accelerating the task of filtering audio data using IR after the IR has been calculated (or manually specified).

In 2013, AMD introduced TrueAudio technology, which used dedicated DSP hardware available on certain AMD GPUs to accelerate some audio functions such as rendering 3D audio using Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTFs), and convolution with static IRs. In contrast, TrueAudio Next uses standard, existing Radeon™ GPU resources to implement more general and highly scalable convolution algorithms, which can be used for a wider range of filters, including convolution reverb with time-varying IRs. As a software library built using OpenCL, TrueAudio Next can also be targeted to CPUs, but it is especially beneficial when it is used with GPU Resource Reservation.

[h1]How is TrueAudio Next useful to Steam® Audio?[/h1]

[b]Indirect Sound[/b]
Steam® Audio uses physics-based simulation to model two ways in which sound travels from a source to a listener. Direct sound is sound that travels in a straight line from the source to the listener, possibly passing through solid objects. Indirect sound is sound that is emitted from the source, bounces off solid objects repeatedly, and then reaches the listener.

Steam® Audio models indirect sound by calculating an IR using ray tracing. This IR is then used in a convolution reverb effect to add indirect sound effects to either individual sound sources (in the case of source-centric convolution reverb) or a submix of sound reaching the listener (in the case of listener-centric convolution reverb).

Simulating and rendering indirect sound is the most computationally intensive part of what Steam® Audio does, and TrueAudio Next helps manage this workload.

[b]Ambisonics[/b]
Source-centric convolution reverb can be directional in nature: somebody else's distant footsteps heard through an open doorway sound more directional than one's own footsteps in a large room, for example. Steam® Audio uses Ambisonics to represent the directional variation of indirect sound. The higher the Ambisonics order, the more spatial detail that can be rendered in the indirect sound. On the other hand, the higher the Ambisonics order, the more IRs that are needed in the convolution reverb effect. For example, 2nd order Ambisonics requires 9 convolutions per source. This too, increases the computational cost of indirect sound.

Note that Steam® Audio does not use TrueAudio Next for applying HRTF-based 3D audio rendering. The computational cost of HRTF processing is significantly lower than that of convolution reverb: thousands of sources can be rendered with HRTF-based 3D audio using a single CPU core.

[h1]Why does Steam® Audio support TrueAudio Next?[/h1]
Steam® Audio's existing CPU-based convolution has sufficient performance for many applications, particularly those that rely heavily on listener-centric reverb. However, with TrueAudio Next, Steam® Audio can offer more flexibility to developers.

There are two main reasons why we chose to support TrueAudio Next in Steam® Audio:
[list]
[*]If we can provide developers with more flexibility in choosing how their audio processing workloads are balanced on a user's PC, we want to do that. TrueAudio Next allows developers to choose how CPU and GPU resources work together to provide a compelling audio experience on the user's PC.
[*]If we can allow developers to offer an optional higher level of audio detail with their existing content on PCs that are powerful enough, we want to do that. With Steam® Audio, developers just specify higher settings to be used if a TAN-capable GPU is installed on the user's PC. Developers do not have to re-author any content to work with TAN. Steam® Audio can be used to seamlessly select either CPU- or GPU-based convolution, depending on the user's hardware configuration.
[/list]
Steam® Audio's support for TrueAudio Next does not in any way restrict Steam® Audio to specific hardware or platforms. We hope that our support for TrueAudio Next encourages hardware and platform vendors to provide more options for developers to balance their audio workloads against graphics, physics, and other workloads, which in turn will help them create better audio experiences for their users.

[h1]What are the benefits of TrueAudio Next?[/h1]

[b]Benefits of GPU convolution[/b]
TAN's OpenCL convolution algorithms move convolution from the CPU to the GPU, and help achieve significant audio processing speedups. This has the following advantages:
[list]
[*]Steam® Audio's CPU-based convolution is highly efficient, and is sufficient for a wide variety of games and VR applications, especially if only using listener-centric reverb. However, TAN allows us to give developers the option of reaching an even higher level of auditory complexity: increasing the number of sources, or the Ambisonics order for indirect sound, or the IR length, etc.
[*]By moving convolution from the CPU to the GPU, the fraction of time spent by the CPU on audio processing can be kept within the CPU budget chosen by the developer. This also frees up more CPU resources for use by other tasks such as physics simulation or AI.
[/list]
[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/52ec0cfcccdbec88f80b1c0ca8e5cb237abc56fb.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]GPU convolution performance vs CPU convolution performance, for 1s IRs, 1st order Ambisonics, 1024-sample frames, and a 48 kHz sampling rate. The performance advantage of GPU convolution increases with number of sources. CPU convolution is usable up to a moderate number of sources; GPU convolution is necessary for large numbers of sources.[/i]

[b]Benefits of resource reservation[/b]
Resource reservation causes TAN's convolution algorithms to run in isolation from any rendering, physics, or other tasks that the GPU is being used for. This has two broad advantages:
[list]
[*]Increasing the number of reserved CUs predictably results in improved performance, even under the heaviest workloads.
[*]Because audio processing does not interfere with graphics, the audio processing does not result in sudden frame rate drops and stuttering.
[*]Because graphics does not interfere with audio processing, rendering a complex scene cannot cause audio processing to slow down, which in turn helps avoid unacceptable clicks, pops, or other audio glitches.
[/list]

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2a62f348cc3fd0ef418e1c072bfd4c09f4626127.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Performance improvements with increasing numbers of reserved CUs, for 1s IRs, 1st order Ambisonics, 1024-sample frames, and a 48 kHz sampling rate. The plot shows the maximum number of sources that can be processed within a 6ms budget. Increasing the number of reserved CUs allows more sources to be processed within the same amount of time.[/i]

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2561bbd971cf7f25e9d4d9395614ef6a9e53da45.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Impact on GPU rendering performance when reserving 4 CUs for TrueAudio Next processing. The plots show the average FPS observed on various GPU benchmarks when run at the same time as a TAN benchmark using Steam® Audio. Measurements obtained using a Radeon™ RX 480 GPU with 4 reserved CUs, 256 total convolution channels and 1.3s IRs. All values are shown as a percentage of a baseline that is obtained when the TAN benchmark is not running. For example, reserving 10% of the available CUs reduces the average FPS in the Timespy benchmark by about 10%.[/i]

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/6a8f38ac7fe4a422ded8afa46b1b99851207206c.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Impact on TAN processing time when heavy graphics workloads are running concurrently. CU reservation limits the impact of heavy graphics workloads on time-sensitive audio processing tasks on the GPU. Measurements obtained using a Radeon™ RX 480 GPU with 4 reserved CUs, 256 total convolution channels, 1.3s IRs, 1024-sample audio frames, and a sampling rate of 48 kHz.[/i]

[h1]How do I enable TrueAudio Next in Steam® Audio?[/h1]

[b]System Requirements[/b]

[table]
[tr]
[th]Supported GPUs[/th]
[th]Operating System[/th]
[th]GPU Drivers[/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]Radeon™ RX 470 Series
Radeon™ RX 480 Series
Radeon™ RX 570 Series
Radeon™ RX 580 Series
Radeon™ R9 Fury
Radeon™ R9 Fury X
Radeon™ Pro Duo
Radeon™ RX Vega 56
Radeon™ RX Vega 64[/td]
[td]Windows 10, 64-bit[/td]
[td]Current Radeon™ Adrenalin Edition drivers

Download location:
[url=http://support.amd.com/en-us/download]http://support.amd.com/en-us/download[/url]
[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[b]Using the Unity Plugin[/b]
To use TAN in a Unity project that uses the Steam® Audio Unity plugin, you must add a Steam® Audio Custom Settings component to the Steam® Audio Manager Settings object in every scene that you wish to use TAN in, and then set Convolution Option to TrueAudio Next. Refer to the documentation for more details on the other settings that are displayed when Convolution Option is set to TrueAudio Next.

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2e44bdcfadb466b163d04099ac5bc15d0bc0fce1.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Enabling TrueAudio Next in the Steam® Audio Unity plugin.[/i]

Steam® Audio allows the developer to select the number of CUs to be reserved and to independently configure the higher-detail settings to be used when TrueAudio Next is available. When TrueAudio Next is not available, CPU convolution with a default configuration can be used seamlessly. TrueAudio Next, along with resource reservation, can also be enabled or disabled on a scene-by-scene basis.

[b]Using the FMOD Studio Plugin[/b]
To use TAN in an FMOD Studio project that is part of a Unity project that uses Steam® Audio FMOD Studio plugin, follow the instructions for enabling TAN in the Steam® Audio Unity plugin. No further action is required.

[b]Using the Unreal Engine 4 Plugin[/b]
To use TAN in an Unreal Engine 4 project, you can simply configure the Steam® Audio plugin settings to use convolution type "AMD TrueAudio Next". This will allow you to configure the number of compute units available for audio processing. No further action is required. 

TAN for Steam® Audio is currently available to users who build from source via [url=https://github.com/EpicGames/UnrealEngine/pull/4478]this pull request on GitHub[/url] (requires membership in the EpicGames organization).

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/6f02467ae0fac0518188c272ff02ad3c6bc5cb25.png[/img]
[b]Figure:[/b] [i]Enabling TrueAudio Next in the Steam® Audio Unreal Engine plugin.[/i]

[b]Using the C API[/b]
To use TAN in an application that directly uses the Steam® Audio C API, you will need to perform two main steps:
[list]
[*][b]Initialize an OpenCL compute device that supports TAN.[/b] To do this, call iplCreateComputeDevice, typically at application startup. In the deviceFilter parameter, set type to IPL_COMPUTEDEVICE_GPU, and requiresTrueAudioNext to IPL_TRUE. This will cause Steam® Audio to try initializing OpenCL to use a GPU that supports TAN. If no such device is found on the user's PC, an error code is returned. The application should test this error code and take appropriate action in case of failure, such as falling back to Steam® Audio's built-in CPU-based convolution. This compute device should be passed to all Steam® Audio API functions that take a computeDevice parameter.

[*][b]Create an Environmental Renderer that uses TAN for convolution.[/b] When calling iplCreateEnvironmentalRenderer to create an environmental renderer, in the renderingSettings parameter, set convolutionType to IPL_CONVOLUTIONTYPE_TRUEAUDIONEXT. If the function returns a status code indicating success, then all subsequently created Convolution Effect objects will use TAN.
[/list]
Note that when using TAN for convolution, iplGetMixedEnvironmentalAudio is much more efficient than calling iplGetWetAudioForConvolutionEffect for each Convolution Effect object separately.

notes.title: Beta 12: FMOD Studio plugin and more
notes.content:
[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/5a32d5027d3c4a30786f004155a7ce2134f4d1d7.png[/img]

We've just released Steam Audio beta 12, and with it, we're excited to introduce our FMOD Studio plugin! This let you use the full range of spatial audio functionality available in Steam Audio -- including HRTF, occlusion, physics-based sound propagation, and baking -- to projects that use FMOD Studio. In addition, beta 12 contains various bug fixes and improvements; see the full release notes at the end of this post for details. Click [url=https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/]here[/url] to download the latest version of Steam Audio, including the FMOD Studio plugin.

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/29b24bbda09b1bddfa440f62570aea8bfa251413.png[/img]

The FMOD Studio plugin is equivalent in functionality to the Unity native audio plugin. Like the Unity plugin, we are releasing the full source code for the FMOD Studio plugin via the [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio]Steam Audio repository on GitHub[/url].

[h1]Platform Support[/h1]
Our official release only provides binaries for 64-bit Windows via our [url=https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/]Downloads[/url] page. Binaries for other platforms, including Linux, macOS, Android, and 32-bit Windows may be built from source, but have not been tested by us, and are not supported at this time.

If you wish to build and test a port of the FMOD Studio plugin to one of the other platforms, we encourage you to open a pull request and contribute your changes back to the community.

[h1]Steam Audio + FMOD Studio + Unity[/h1]
If your project uses FMOD Studio with Unity, you need to import the following:
[olist]
[*]The FMOD Studio plugin should be imported into your FMOD Studio project (or to another location of your choice, see the documentation for details). This lets you add Steam Audio effects to FMOD Studio events.
[*]The Unity plugin (SteamAudio.unitypackage) should be imported into your Unity project. This lets you specify acoustic geometry and materials, adjust simulation settings, and bake sound propagation and reverb effects.
[*]The Unity + FMOD Studio plugin (SteamAudio_FMODStudio.unitypackage) should be imported into your Unity project. This allows the Unity plugin to exchange scene-related information with the FMOD Studio plugin.
[/olist]
As always, we welcome you to report bugs via the [url=http://steamcommunity.com/app/596420/discussions/]Steam Audio forums[/url] and [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio/issues]GitHub issue tracker[/url]. We also welcome bug fixes (and ports) via GitHub pull requests.

[h1]Full Release Notes[/h1]
[list]
[*][b](FMOD Studio)[/b] Steam Audio is now available as a plugin for FMOD Studio 1.10.01+. Source code and Windows binaries are available for download; other platforms may be built from source.
[*][b](FMOD Studio, Unity)[/b] The Steam Audio Unity plugin now supports using FMOD Studio as your audio engine. This is required if using the Steam Audio plugin in FMOD Studio.
[*][b](Unity)[/b] Fixed a bug where unoccluded sound is incorrectly played in the first few frames after an occluded Audio Source starts playing.
[*][b](Unity)[/b] Eliminated intermittent CPU spikes when using the Steam Audio Source component.
[*][b](FMOD Studio, Unity, Unreal)[/b] Documentation format changed to single page embedded HTML.
[/list]

notes.title: Beta 10: Quality Improvements, Unreal Android, Pull Requests, and More!
notes.content:
我們在今天推出的 Steam Audio 測試版版本 10 將帶來顯著的品質提升，以及針對 Unreal Enging 4 整合的更新。另外，我們也正在實驗以 GitHub 更迅速地將 UE4 更新開放給開發人員的方式。

[h1]品質提升的要項[/h1]
測試版版本 10 提升了聲音傳遞與重現的品質。首先，我們大幅減少了聲射線的洩漏，讓間接聲響能對應密封的幾何。第二，我們修正了產生次要聲射線時的程式錯誤，因此增強了聽者能接收到的能量。第三，我們標準化了所有聲學探測器的脈衝回應內插，應能在轉譯重現後的效果時去除飽和度過高或過低的脈衝回應。最後，我們最佳化了處理聲學探測器的方式，讓使用者在製作大型場景時能迅速做出大量（約 100k 以上）的探測器。

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/866603249ab8a49878882bd555f6949884fb20a9.png[/img]

[h1]針對 Unreal Engine 的改良[/h1]
我們的 Unreal Engine 整合現支援 Android 的音場定位與聲響遮蔽，也更適用於處理大型場景。第一，我們將主要的資料來源（場景輸出和脈衝回應重現）移到了磁碟檔案上，藉此提升儲存和載入階層時變慢的速度。第二，我們在編輯器模式中新增了分頁，讓使用者能快速找到 Steam Audio 外掛程式提供的功能。最後，我們替場景中所有的靜態網格元素（Static Mesh Actor）添加了新增 / 移除聲子幾何的按鈕。方便吧！

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/2fd8c93a470abbc2c11a3859e6ceb0078b029a98.png[/img]

[h1]公開的 GitHub 提取要求（Pull Request）[/h1]
本次釋出最後一項主要變更是改為使用 GitHub 提取要求來釋出對 Unreal Engine 整合的更新。雖然大部分使用者將透過 Epic Launcher 取得官方釋出，但如果你是個追求新奇刺激的人，便能在搶所有人之前用到最新最棒的功能。另外值得一提的是，已經有使用者提交了外掛程式的問題修正，而我們對這些貢獻更是萬分感激！

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/linkfilter/?url=https://github.com/EpicGames/UnrealEngine/pull/4134]請點擊這裡檢視測試版版本 10 的提取要求[/url]

[h1]完整變更列表[/h1]
[list]
[*]（C API、Unreal Engine、Unity）變更探測器批次的收尾方式（Finalization），以能處理大量的探測器
[*]（C API、Unreal Engine、Unity）修正產生次要聲射線時造成能量大量流失的程式錯誤
[*]（C API、Unreal Engine、Unity）標準化資料內插，讓重現後的資料更加平滑地轉譯
[*]（C API、Unreal Engine、Unity）修正間接模擬的聲射線洩漏
[*]（C API）將自訂聲射線追蹤器的最近撞擊回呼改為傳回撞擊點的材質，而非材質的索引
[*]（Unreal Engine）支援 Android 上的音場定位與聲響遮蔽
[*]（Unreal Engine）新增編輯器模式，以能便捷的取用 Steam Audio 的功能
[*]（Unreal Engine）在所有靜態網格元素上添加新增 / 移除聲子幾何元件的按鈕
[*]（Unreal Engine）新增將場景輸出為 .obj 的按鈕，以用於偵錯
[*]（Unreal Engine）移除聲子場景元素，以利於輸出成檔案
[*]（Unreal Engine）產生與重現偵測器時將把資料寫入磁碟，以避免載入與儲存貼圖檔案時過度緩慢
[*]（Unreal Engine）修正輸出場景時錯誤的材質索引
[*]（Unreal Engine）在聲子場景中顯示三角形的數量
[*]（Unreal Engine）改善資料大小的顯示方式
[*]（Unity）修正使用 Steam Audio 混音器的回傳（Return）效果時造成吸聲幾何無法隨著場景改變的程式問題，該問題會產生錯誤的間接聲響
[/list]

notes.title: Beta 10: Quality Improvements, Unreal Android, Pull Requests, and More!
notes.content:
Today we are releasing Steam Audio beta 10, which includes significant quality improvements and updates to the Unreal Engine 4 integration. We are also experimenting with using GitHub to get UE4 updates out to developers more quickly.

[h1]Core Quality Improvements[/h1]
Beta 10 focuses on quality improvements to propagation and baking. First, we greatly reduced ray leakage so that indirect sound will respect watertight geometry. Second, we fixed a bug in secondary ray generation that will result in a greater level of energy reaching the listener. Third, we normalized impulse response interpolation across acoustic probes, which should eliminate over or under saturated IRs when rendering baked effects. Finally, we optimized the way we handle probes so that users can quickly generate many (~100k+) probes if they're working with a large scene.

[img]http://cdn.edgecast.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/866603249ab8a49878882bd555f6949884fb20a9.png[/img]

[h1]Unreal Engine Improvements[/h1]
Our Unreal Engine integration now supports Android for spatialization and occlusion. The integration is also in a much better position to handle large scenes. First, we shifted major sources of data (scene export and baked IRs) to files on disk, which will fix any slowdowns users were experiencing when saving and loading levels. Second, we added an editor mode tab so that users can quickly find the functionality exposed by the Steam Audio plugin. Finally, we added buttons for adding/removing Phonon Geometry to all static mesh actors in the scene. Handy!

notes.title: Blog: Steam Audio Unity Native Plugin
notes.content:
就在剛剛我們[url=http://steamcommunity.com/games/596420/announcements/detail/1443820118333481341]釋出了 Steam Audio 2.0-beta.7[/url] 更新，為 Unity 的 Steam Audio 外掛程式帶來了重大的改變。這次更新以後，Steam Audio 將使用 Unity原生的音訊外掛程式框架，以更緊密地整合 Unity 音訊引擎的完整功能，也為使用者帶來簡化、一致的作業流程。

由於本次更新的大幅改動，使用 Steam Audio 測試版版本 6 或更舊的 Unity 專案須重新整合 Steam Audio。大部分狀況下，過程應相當直觀，並能帶來多項好處：

[h1]混音器外掛程式[/h1]
使用 Unity原生的音訊外掛程式框架的主要好處之一便是可以建立[b]混音器外掛程式[/b]。這些效果可以在場景的混音圖表中，透過任何混音器分類節點套用至音訊流程上。

如此一來便可很省事地將 Steam Audio 的效果套用到分類中所有聲響上。例如說，你可利用 Steam Audio 的殘響效果，將物理基礎的殘響套用至名為 Reverb 的混音器分類中所有的聲響：
[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/fa2e97e6fa81d53d8392f0790a0e2a274e360500.png[/img]

由於原版音訊外掛程式框架的局限，Steam Audio 測試版版本 6 或更舊的版本便無法如此設定。

[h1]濕性混音[/h1]
Unity 可在混音器分類的音效上開啟[b]濕性混音[/b]。開啟後，在輸出音訊效果時，便能控制要混合多少的乾性（未修正的）訊號與濕性（經修正的）訊號。

比方說，若使用 Steam Audio 殘響，便能啟用濕性混音來控制要套入多少物理基礎的殘響：

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/e3b2ba4a1c278fa618d1929082ec7c32c3a9e72d.png[/img]

[h1]效能[/h1]
Unity 的原生音訊外掛程式是以原生 C++ 程式碼實作而成，與原版以 C# 寫成的音訊外掛程式框架相較之下，所使用的 CPU 較少。原版的音訊外掛程式得在受管理的 .NET 程式碼與未受管理的原生程式碼之間封送音訊資料，造成意料之外極高的效能額外負荷。由於 Steam Audio 已轉為使用原生的音訊外掛程式框架，便能避免此類的效能低下。 

[h1]便利性[/h1]
最後，使用原生音效外掛程式框架也表示，假如你只想要 HRTF 基礎的 3D 音效，你只需要在專案中將音場定位器（Spatializer）外掛程式設為 Steam Audio、選擇一些 Audio Source，再勾選音場定位（Spatialize）就完成了，不必附加任何元件，也不須調整設定。

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/4700a0cba9fe12da20c9e4864a7a2dd31b3573b3.png[/img]

當然，如果你想使用 Steam Audio 的進階功能，例如聲響遮蔽、傳輸、間接聲響，或聲響重現，設定起來也相當簡單：只要附加上所需的 Steam Audio 元件即可。

隨著 Unity 團隊持續改良他們的音效引擎，基於原生音訊外掛程式框架的 Steam Audio 便能使用 Unity 最新增加的音訊功能。

還有，如同以往，如果你在使用 Steam Audio 測試版版本 7 時遇到任何問題，請至討論區或 GitHub 回報。

notes.title: Blog: Steam Audio Unity Native Plugin
notes.content:
We have just [url=http://steamcommunity.com/games/596420/announcements/detail/1443820118333481341]released Steam Audio 2.0-beta.7[/url], and it brings a major change to the Steam Audio plugin for Unity. From here on out, Steam Audio will use the [b]native audio plugin[/b] framework for Unity, which allows for tighter integration with the complete feature set of Unity's audio engine, and a simplified, consistent workflow for users.

Because of the far-reaching nature of this update, you will have to reintegrate Steam Audio into existing Unity projects that use Steam Audio beta 6 or earlier. In most cases, this should be a straightforward process, which brings with it several benefits.

[h1]Audio Mixer Plugins[/h1]
One of the main advantages of Unity's native audio plugin framework is that it allows the creation of [b]mixer plugins[/b]. These are effects that can be applied to audio flowing through any given Mixer Group node in a scene's Audio Mixer graph.

This lets you efficiently apply Steam Audio effects to a group of sounds; for example, you can use the Steam Audio Reverb effect to apply physics-based reverb to all sounds that mix into the Mixer Group called Reverb:

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/fa2e97e6fa81d53d8392f0790a0e2a274e360500.png[/img]

This was not possible using Steam Audio beta 6 or older, due to the limitations of the legacy audio plugin framework.

[h1]Wet Mixing[/h1]
Unity lets you enable [b]wet mixing[/b] on any audio effect attached to a Mixer Group. This lets you control how much of the dry (unmodified) signal is mixed with the wet (modified) signal when generating the audio effect's output.

For example, with Steam Audio Reverb, you can enable wet mixing to control how much physics-based reverb is applied:

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/e3b2ba4a1c278fa618d1929082ec7c32c3a9e72d.png[/img]

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Unity's native audio plugin framework is implemented in native C++ code, which results in lower CPU usage than the legacy audio plugin framework, which was written in C#. The legacy audio plugins had to marshal audio data between managed .NET code and unmanaged native code, which resulted in a surprisingly high performance overhead. By switching Steam Audio to the native audio plugin framework, we have eliminated this performance hit.

[h1]Ease of Use[/h1]
Finally, using the native audio plugin framework means that if you just want HRTF-based 3D audio, all you have to do is set Steam Audio as the spatializer plugin in your project, select a bunch of Audio Sources, and check Spatialize. That's it: no components to attach, no settings to configure.

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/4700a0cba9fe12da20c9e4864a7a2dd31b3573b3.png[/img]

Of course, if you want to use the advanced features of Steam Audio, like occlusion, transmission, indirect sound, or baking, those remain easy to set up too: just attach the necessary Steam Audio components.

As the Unity team continues to improve their audio engine, the migration to the native audio plugin framework will allow Steam Audio to make use of the latest audio features added to Unity.

And, as always, let us know in the forums or on GitHub if you run into any issues when using Steam Audio beta 7.

[h1]統一的聲響重現[/h1]

現在可在全新的獨立視窗中選取任何聲子源和聽者中心殘響並重現。當你的場景有所變更、需要重新重現多個音源時，此視窗便非常重要。方便吧！

傳輸會在聲音穿過障礙物時，根據障礙物的材質屬性過濾聲音。過濾可依頻率而有所不同，比方說，當聲音穿過牆壁時，高頻率被減弱的幅度會比低頻率來得更大。

notes.title: Steam Audio for Unreal 4.17
notes.content:
The next iteration of Steam Audio for Unreal Engine 4 is now available in the 4.17 Preview. This release is focused on stability and bugfixes, but provides some new features and ease-of-use improvements. Highlights include a consolidated baking menu, support for frequency-dependent transmission, and fully transformable probe volumes.

[h1]Consolidated Baking[/h1]

All Phonon Sources and listener-centric reverb may be selected and baked inside of a new standalone window. This is very important to have when your scene changes and you need to re-bake many sources. Convenient!

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/185ff4a6ae8c849a9517e93f61c1dac14c1df961.png[/img]

[h1]Frequency-dependent Transmission[/h1]

Transmission allows sound to be filtered as it passes through occluding geometry, based on the material properties of the occluding object. The filtering can depend on frequency, so for example high frequencies may be attenuated more than low frequencies as the sound passes through a wall.

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/1e39819d6efb5ac828c6ed3b4f7241eb8f4d84e9.png[/img]

[h1]Transformable Probe Volumes[/h1]

Previously, we required Phonon Probe Volumes to be axis-aligned, even though the transform gizmo allowed for arbitrary rotations and scaling. Our updated API now supports arbitrary transformations, so you can transform your probe volumes to better fit your scene geometry. The probes will be generated in alignment with the volume's local coordinate system.

[img]http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/27920370/46a4306ffeecab3609447452fd68e9c4d5595966.png[/img]

[h1]Full Changelist[/h1]

[list]
  [*] Fixed packaging compilation errors.
  [*] Phonon Probe Volumes are set to NoCollide collision profile by default.
  [*] Phonon Probe Volumes may be arbitrarily rotated, scaled, and translated.
  [*] Consolidated baking into a single window. Users can select multiple sources to bake at once.
  [*] Added support for transmission.
  [*] Added Phonon Scene actor for scene export - this removes need for external .phononscene file and simplifies packaging.
  [*] Added support for multichannel output.
  [*] Fixed buffer size related crashes.
  [*] Added Win32 support.
[/list]

Be sure to grab the [url=https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-audio/releases/download/v2.0-beta.6/steamaudio_manual_unreal_2.0-beta.6.pdf]updated manual[/url], and swing by the forums with any questions you might have!
